newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW -Pitney Bowes sets digital copiers.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW -Pitney Bowes sets digital copiers.

text.p: Pitney Bowes Inc is hoping to trade on its longstanding reputation in the field of postage-meter machines to enter a more modern field: digital copiers.

Murray Martin, president of Pitney Bowes Copier Systems, said Tuesday that the company hopes the longstanding relationships it has built up over the years through its postage-meter business will come into play as the company seeks to carve out a niche in this fast-growing market.
"We have millions of customers thorugh the traditional mail operations," he said. "We are leveraging on strengths there."

On Tuesday, Pitney Bowes began marketing two versions of the copier: a full-color copier, called CD6000, going for $70,000, and a black-and-white version, known as DL350, for $17,500. The copiers are made by Minolta Co Ltd but will carry the Pitney Bowes name.
The goal is to persuade businesses to buy the copiers, which can be integrated into their computer networks, to handle printing jobs that are now sent out to printing contractors.
Unlike analog copiers, which require the user to physically place the document to be copied onto or into the machine, digital copiers can be used manually or through a company's computer network.
They are being marketed to companies, organizations and print shops that create 1,800 or more color prints a month.
But Martin says the new product isn't being reserved solely for the largest companies.
"The color market has been a very specialized market for some time -- really a higher priced product," Martin said. "We're really now moving into the next generation."
Martin declined to specify what kind of market share the company anticipated. However, he said Pitney Bowes hopes to be among the top three producers of digital copiers.
As it stands now, copiers account for about 10 percent of Pitney Bowes' sales, and the company has captured about four percent of the overall copier market.
The new product is not expected to affect the company's revenues or earnings until the end of the 1997 fiscal year, he said.
Peter Enderlin, an analyst with Smith Barney, said Pitney Bowes is "sort of following what everyone else is doing."
Companies long dominant in the field, such as Xerox Corp and Canon Inc, may not consider Pitney Bowes in and of itself a threat, Enderlin said.
However, there are a growing number of Japanese and American companies interested in breaking into the market that could eventually shrink their hold on the area, Enderlin said.
Enderlin said Pitney Bowes' experience in the marketplace may serve it well in correctly judging the market for digital copiers.
"They have enough experience in the marketplace and have been selling analog copiers long enough they can judge the market," he said.

Xerox spokesman Jeffrey Simek said the company is not worried by the prospect of increased competition. Xerox makes a host of digital copiers -- from one that churns out five copies a minute to the Docucolor 40, which costs about three times as much as Pitney Bowes' CD6000 but makes about 40 copies a minute.

"We are already in one of the most competitive industries in the world, and we grew up with competition all around us," Simek said. "Our intent is to lead the industry, and we will continue to strive to do so."
